desc:
Start with an empty singly linked list and apply a script of edits. Each edit is a triple [type, a, b]:

  • [0, v, 0]: insert a new node with value v at the head.
  • [1, v, 0]: append a new node with value v at the tail.
  • [2, i, v]: insert a new node with value v so that it becomes the node at index i (0-based). If i equals the current length this appends; if i is larger than the length the edit is ignored.
  • [3, i, 0]: delete the node at index i. If there is no node at that index the edit is ignored.

Return the values of the final list from head to tail. For example [[0,5,0],[1,7,0],[2,1,9],[3,0,0]] builds [5], [5,7], [5,9,7] and finally [9,7].
hints: Every edit is one of the standard linked list moves: insert at the front, insert at the back, insert in the middle, delete.
A dummy node placed before the head removes all special cases for 'index 0': to edit position i you stop at the node just before it.

Keep a dummy head and optionally a tail pointer. For index edits walk i steps from the dummy to find the predecessor; if you run off the end before taking i steps (insert) or find no node after the predecessor (delete), ignore the edit.
editorial: Use a dummy node whose next is the real head. Then inserting at the head is inserting after the dummy, and for any index i the predecessor is the node reached after i steps from the dummy. Insert: link a new node after the predecessor. Delete: set pred.next = pred.next.next when pred.next exists.

The walk can only go as far as the list is long, so an index beyond the length is detected when the walk hits null early (insert) or when the predecessor has no successor (delete). Each edit costs O(i) (O(1) for the head, and O(n) for an append unless you keep a tail pointer), so the whole script is O(q · n) in the worst case, which is fine for 3,000 edits.
